summary: Creates a shared rhythm for the wider King’s experience, bringing together the major agendas that shape student life so activity, opportunity and support are better coordinated around student need, capacity and key moments in the journey.
detailSummary:
King’s will create a clearer and more intentional rhythm across the wider student experience, helping the institution coordinate opportunity, participation, support and connection around the moments when students are most likely to need and value them.

The functional milestones of university life, including enrolment, arrival, assessment, progression, return to study and completion, will provide a flexible spine. These moments do not occur at the same time for every student, so the framework will recognise common types of transition and need while accommodating different programmes, calendars and patterns of study.

Around this spine, King’s will bring together the major agendas that shape student life, including employability, student success, wellbeing, community and connection, belonging and participation beyond the course. Stakeholders across these areas, alongside faculties, services, KCLSU and student communities, will be convened to consider the student journey collectively rather than through separate organisational calendars.

This shared planning rhythm will help King’s identify where priorities reinforce one another, where activity competes for student attention, where important needs are underserved, and where particular moments provide opportunities for stronger institutional coordination. Existing provision can then be timed, connected and surfaced more intelligently, while new activity is commissioned selectively where genuine gaps or strategic opportunities emerge.

External, cultural, civic, religious and place-based moments with genuine convening power can also form part of the rhythm, alongside a small number of deliberately created King’s moments where giving an important transition, opportunity or achievement greater visibility and shared meaning would add value.

King’s Edge will provide the orchestration layer for this work, maintaining the shared student-journey framework, convening stakeholders around the annual planning cycle, connecting evidence with delivery, and helping the wider institution increasingly plan around students rather than around separate organisational agendas.
problemSolved: The wider King’s experience is shaped by multiple important agendas, including employability, student success, wellbeing, belonging, community, connection and participation beyond the course, but these are often planned and delivered through separate organisational cycles. Students can therefore encounter competing demands at some points in the year, limited invitation or support at others, and a wider experience that feels fragmented rather than intentionally shaped around their journey.
whatChanges: King’s establishes a shared student-journey rhythm through which the major agendas shaping student experience are considered together. Faculties, services, KCLSU and other partners coordinate activity around student need, capacity and key transitions, improving the timing and connection of existing provision and identifying where new activity would add value.

caseForChange.problem:
The academic journey gives students a relatively clear sense of progression through teaching, assessment and formal milestones. The wider experience of being a King’s student is much less deliberately organised.

Students encounter opportunities, communities, services and interventions shaped by a range of important institutional priorities, including employability, student success, wellbeing, belonging, community and connection. Each has legitimate objectives and often strong provision behind it. However, these agendas are frequently planned through different organisational structures and calendars rather than from a shared view of the student journey.

The result can be an experience that is richer in provision than it is coherent in practice. Activity can cluster around highly visible moments such as Welcome, multiple priorities can compete for attention at periods when students have limited capacity, and quieter parts of the year can offer fewer recognisable invitations to reconnect, explore opportunities or seek support.

Students whose circumstances make participation less straightforward can be particularly affected. Those who commute, work significant hours, have caring responsibilities, study at a distance or miss early opportunities to connect may find few obvious points of re-entry into the wider King’s experience.

Without a shared institutional rhythm, strong individual provision can therefore combine into a student experience that feels fragmented, poorly timed and harder to navigate than it needs to be.
caseForChange.opportunity:
King’s can organise the wider student experience more intentionally around the changing needs, capacity and priorities of students.

Functional milestones such as enrolment, arrival, assessment, progression, return and completion can provide a flexible spine for understanding the student journey. Around these moments, King’s can consider when students are likely to need orientation, connection, opportunity, recovery, confidence, reflection, celebration or support.

The greater opportunity is to use this framework to bring together the major agendas that currently shape student life separately. Stakeholders responsible for employability, student success, wellbeing, community and connection, belonging and wider participation can work alongside faculties, services, KCLSU and student communities to consider the year collectively.

This creates a shared basis for identifying where different priorities can reinforce one another, where the institution is creating unnecessary competition for student attention, where significant gaps exist, and where a coordinated response could create more value than isolated activity.

Evidence about participation, reach, student experience and outcomes can increasingly inform this planning cycle. Existing activity can be coordinated and surfaced at more useful moments, while commissioning can be focused on gaps or opportunities that the existing ecology does not meet.

The result is not a single universal calendar or centrally controlled programme of events. It is a shared institutional framework through which King’s becomes better at shaping the wider experience around students rather than expecting students to make sense of multiple disconnected institutional agendas.
caseForChange.whyNow:
Students are balancing study with increasing levels of paid work, commuting, caring responsibilities, financial pressure and other demands on their time. This makes the timing, clarity and accessibility of opportunities and support increasingly important.

At the same time, King’s is strengthening several major dimensions of the student experience, including graduate futures, student success, wellbeing, community, belonging and participation beyond the course. As these agendas develop, there is a growing risk that individually valuable activity becomes harder for students to navigate if it is not considered collectively.

King’s Edge is also moving from defining and growing the Beyond Course ecology towards actively stewarding it. Work elsewhere in the programme will make opportunities more visible, improve participation evidence and create richer physical and digital invitations into student life. The next requirement is therefore to ensure that these assets are activated through a coherent understanding of when and why students are most likely to engage.

Creating a shared rhythm now gives King’s a practical mechanism for connecting these developments and for bringing stakeholders together around a common view of the student journey.
caseForChange.intendedChange:
Students experience a more coherent and recognisable rhythm across their wider King’s experience, with repeated opportunities to connect, participate, explore, recover, reflect and move forward at moments that better match their needs and capacity.

The major agendas shaping student life are increasingly planned in relation to one another. Stakeholders across employability, student success, wellbeing, community and connection, belonging and wider participation regularly consider the student journey together, identifying where their priorities intersect and where greater coordination would improve the experience students encounter.

Faculties, services, KCLSU and student communities gain a shared framework for planning around student need rather than separate organisational calendars. Existing activity is timed and connected more intentionally, competing demands become more visible, and gaps can be addressed through targeted commissioning.

Over time, participation and student-experience evidence helps King’s refine this rhythm and understand which forms of coordination make the greatest difference.

The result is a wider King’s experience that feels increasingly intentional, joined-up and easier to enter and re-enter, while making better collective use of the substantial opportunities, communities and support that already exist across the institution.
